data.title: David's Bridal plans to spin off its AI-powered Pearl platform
data.description:
In 2025, David’s Bridal’s Shopify transition paved the way for an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) reimagining of its Pearl wedding planner — and now, the company has plans to spin off Pearl as its own entity.

K&F Growth Acquisition Corp. II, as special purposed acquisition company, announced alongside David’s Bridal, that the two companies had signed a nonbinding letter of intent to carry out a process to that would see Pearl go public.

Ultimately, their plan also calls for Pearl to eventually own David’s Bridal’s brand and intellectual property.

David’s Bridal is No. 460 in the Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

David’s Bridal is also No. 178 in Digital Commerce 360 and ReFiBuy’s AI Commerce Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

data.title: Salesforce to acquire Braze for $5.66 billion to expand AI-powered marketing
data.description:
Salesforce plans to acquire Braze for $5.66 billion, making an artificial intelligence (AI) play for technology to help brands respond to shopper behavior in real time.

Under the definitive agreement announced Oct. 20, Braze shareholders would receive $47.50 per share in cash. That represents a roughly 58% premium over the stock’s Oct. 19 closing price.

Salesforce expects the acquisition to strengthen its Marketing Cloud business and broader AI offerings.

“Braze was built to turn live customer behavior into personalized engagement at scale,” said Patrick Stokes, president of applications and marketing at Salesforce, in the acquisition announcement. “Bringing that capability together with Salesforce Marketing Cloud, CRM and Data 360 will deliver that wow moment in every customer interaction.”

The transaction is expected to close during Salesforce’s fiscal 2028, which runs from Feb. 1, 2027, through Jan. 31, 2028. The deal remains subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals. Salesforce said it does not expect the acquisition to affect its fiscal 2027 financial guidance.

In North America, 78 of the Top 2000 online retailers use Salesforce as their ecommerce platform, according to Digital Commerce 360 data. Together, those retailers generated more than $192.60 billion in web sales in 2025. The Top 2000 is Digital Commerce 360’s database ranking North America’s largest online retailers by annual ecommerce sales.

What Salesforce gains from Braze’s AI capabilities

New York-based Braze specializes in personalized marketing across mobile apps, websites, email and other digital channels. Using real-time customer data and AI, its platform helps brands optimize the message, timing and channel for customer interactions.

Braze would bring considerable scale to Salesforce’s marketing business. Its platform serves roughly 2,770 customers, including Urban Outfitters, Instacart and Canva. Urban Outfitters is No. 29 in the Top 2000.

In a LinkedIn post on Oct. 20, Braze co-founder and chief technology officer Jon Hyman shared that the platform engages 9 billion monthly active users across its customer base. In 2025, Braze also handled “about 4.5 trillion messages and other actions to consumers,” he wrote.

A key part of the deal is BrazeAI, which combines predictive, generative and agentic AI. According to Braze, the tools can anticipate customer behavior, generate marketing content and optimize when, where and how brands reach shoppers.

How Salesforce plans to integrate Braze

For Salesforce, Braze could fill a gap in its existing marketing business.

The acquisition would give Salesforce “a real-time engagement layer that its marketing business has historically lacked,” Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, told Reuters.

Salesforce plans to connect Braze’s real-time marketing technology with Customer 360, its suite of customer data and applications spanning sales, marketing, commerce and service. The ecommerce platform and software provider expects the combination to strengthen Marketing Cloud, which businesses use to manage marketing campaigns.

With access to Salesforce’s customer data, Braze’s technology could help marketers “adapt engagement as customers browse, buy, and use products,” according to the acquisition announcement.

Salesforce also expects Braze’s AI capabilities to work alongside Agentforce, its platform for deploying AI agents that can make decisions and carry out tasks. The combination could help businesses better coordinate marketing with ecommerce, sales and customer service, Salesforce said.

Meanwhile, Braze CEO and co-founder Bill Magnuson said Salesforce’s technology, reach and partner network would help the company “bring more of our vision to market sooner.”

In an Oct. 20 LinkedIn post, Magnuson also said he would remain CEO and that the company would continue operating as Braze.

How retailers are using Braze to drive sales

Some retailers are already reporting higher engagement and conversion rates from campaigns using Braze’s technology.

Grove Collaborative, a sustainability-focused online retailer, switched to Braze after its previous marketing platform couldn’t support real-time personalization. The system had also crashed on Thanksgiving Eve, according to a Braze case study.

Integrating Braze with its Shopify storefront allowed Grove to automate personalized reminders and product suggestions for shoppers who browsed without buying. The resulting campaign generated a 10% checkout rate, a 41% add-to-cart rate and a 3% click-through rate, according to Braze.

E.l.f. Beauty Inc. offers another example. The beauty retailer partnered with Braze and Stitch to expand its mobile marketing efforts and boost engagement with its loyalty program, Beauty Squad.

With help from the two companies, e.l.f. expanded its use of push notifications and personalized in-app campaigns to encourage customers to return to its mobile app. Between March and September 2023, monthly mobile app usage increased 125%, according to a separate Braze case study.

The retailer also added push notifications to its existing loyalty emails, reminding Beauty Squad members to redeem rewards before they expired. Those efforts, alongside other support from Braze, contributed to a 58% year-over-year increase in loyalty offer redemptions in 2024, according to the study.

Grove ranks No. 256 in the Top 2000, while e.l.f. Beauty ranks No. 328.

Salesforce expands AI capabilities through acquisitions

The Braze deal is part of Salesforce’s push to expand its AI offerings through in-house development and acquisitions.

That strategy comes as Salesforce’s existing AI business gains traction. In its fiscal second quarter, Agentforce annual recurring revenue surpassed $1.5 billion, up 240% year over year. Combined with Data 360, annual recurring revenue reached $3.9 billion, according to the company’s earnings results.

Meanwhile, the company has made several other sizable acquisitions this year. In September, it completed its $3.6 billion deal to acquire Fin, which develops AI agents for handling customer service inquiries.

That same month, it acquired Contentful for roughly $1.5 billion to support more personalized customer experiences.

More recently, Salesforce announced an agreement to acquire Listen Labs, which uses AI agents to conduct customer research and analyze feedback. Financial terms were not disclosed.

data.title: Fastenal digital and automation efforts power Q3 sales growth
data.description:
Fastenal’s CEO credited digital investments and new efficiencies from automation as the industrial products distributor announced that sales grew 15.5% year over year in its fiscal third quarter ended Sept. 30.

In addition, the company cited large customers, pricing actions and “broad-based demand across core end markets” in its Q3 earnings announcement.

Its net sales totaled $2.46 billion, up from $2.13 billion a year ago. As that happened, Fastenal’s operating margin increased by 90 basis points, reaching 21.5% for the quarter, with operating income up by $90 million year over year.

Jeffery Watts, the president and CEO at Fastenal, called operating income growth “the largest year-over-year increase in a single quarter in Fastenal’s history,” during an Oct. 14 earnings call with investors.

Fastenal’s growth and digital footprint in Q3

Assessing the most important drivers behind Fastenal’s business in Q3, Watts first noted accelerated growth in his presentation.

“Second, we converted that growth into higher operating margin and faster earnings growth,” he explained. “And third, the quarter was driven mainly by market share gains through our key account strategy and new contract wins.”

As sales improved, Fastenal’s digital footprint, which includes its inventory management systems FASTBin and FASTVend, accounted for 61.4% of total sales, according to Watts. He noted that digital sales grew 16% during Q3, “faster than the company overall.”

“When customers transact digitally, orders are more accurate, there’s less manual work on both sides, and the relationship becomes much more integrated,” Watts stated.

He added that sales through FASTBin and FASTVend alone were up by “approximately 18%.”

Fastenal’s approach to automation and replenishment

Watts used the Q3 earnings call to highlight a specific case where his company used its Fastenal Managed Inventory (FMI) system to improve automation and replenishment outcomes for a customer, which his case study characterized as a manufacturer with a 20-year-old supply model.

“In this example, we had a new customer that is experiencing direct material stockouts, supply chain shortages and limited control over product consumption,” Watts said. “As their business grew, those challenges became even more significant.”

After assessing the customer’s problems, which Watts described as “a manual, inconsistent system with limited automation, limited digital visibility and physical organization,” Fastenal deployed its set of solutions and reorganized the manufacturer’s crib and storage areas.

“We installed clearly labeled barcoded bins, deployed our FMI technology, established planograms and connected the customer to FAST360 to really provide greater visibility across their facility,” he stated. “We also established KPIs to measure ongoing performance.”

Ultimately, he said Fastenal was able to increase the customer’s digital visibility “from 0% to 99%,” automating replenishment and eliminating stockouts, saving employees time in the process.

“Over time, we expect the solution to generate anywhere between 25% to 30% in overall cost savings,” he added.

Percentage changes may not align exactly with dollar figures due to rounding. Check back for more earnings reports. Here’s last quarter’s update about Fastenal digital sales.

data.title: 1-800-Flowers.com sells two business units to PlanetArt
data.description:
Less than one month after a final deal was announced, 1-800-Flowers.com confirmed that the sale of its PersonalizationMall.com and Things Remembered units to PlanetArt is now complete.

1-800-Flowers.com’s sale to the technology platform marks a step forward during a challenging year for the flowers and gifts retailer as it seeks to focus its business priorities and address falling revenue.

1-800-Flowers.com is No. 67 in the Top 1000 Database. The database tracks North America’s leading online retailers based on their annual ecommerce sales and more.

1-800-Flowers.com is also No. 76 in Digital Commerce 360 and ReFiBuy’s AI Commerce Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

1-800-Flowers.com web sales by year

Why 1-800-Flowers.com sold PersonalizationMall.com and Things Remembered to PlanetArt

“The sale of PersonalizationMall.com enables us to further sharpen our portfolio focus, strengthen our financial position and create additional capacity to invest in the strategic initiatives we believe offer the greatest opportunity to drive improved performance and long-term growth,” said Adolfo Villagomez, CEO at 1-800-Flowers.com, in a released statement on Sept. 29. “As we continue to simplify our business, we are taking a disciplined approach to where ownership creates strategic value and where partnerships can provide a more efficient way to serve our customers.”

Villagomez framed the move as part of a wider effort to correct course at the company.

“This transaction reflects that approach and provides us with greater financial flexibility as we continue executing our transformation and positioning the Company for sustainable, profitable growth,” he stated. “We believe PlanetArt is a strong strategic fit for PersonalizationMall.com and Things Remembered and is well positioned to support the business’s continued growth and success.”

Following the sale, 1-800-Flowers.com expected to reach a deal with PlanetArt that would result in 1-800-Flowers.com continuing to offer some PersonalizationMall.com products.

Are 1-800-Flowers.com’s digital sales growing?

“Throughout fiscal 2026, we strengthened our leadership team, simplified our organization, began to modernize our digital and marketing capabilities, improved operational efficiency, and increasingly put the customer at the center of everything we do,” Villagomez told investors during a Sept. 10 earnings call.

Total ecommerce sales for 1-800-Flowers.com fell by 13.1% year over year to $1.27 billion in results from its fiscal 2026 ended June 28. Over the same period, total revenue declined 10.8% to $1.50 billion.

Villagomez arrived at 1-800-Flowers.com as CEO in 2025, with his background leading online efforts at Home Depot as a prominent part of his résumé. Since then, he has focused on modernization and efficiencies to execute a turnaround.

“As we enter fiscal 2027, accelerating the recovery of our revenue trends is our highest priority,” he said in September. “We will continue building these capabilities while increasingly putting them to work to improve customer acquisition, engagement, and retention and to drive better business performance over time.”

data.title: American Express launches framework to verify AI shopping agent purchases
data.description:
American Express has published a new framework that can help card issuers verify purchases made by artificial intelligence (AI)-powered shopping agents.

The payments company released its Intent Intelligence framework on Tuesday, Oct. 13. With the system, Amex describes how to record a shopper’s purchase instructions before AI agents can buy products or services on the shopper’s behalf.

Card issuers can use those records to help detect fraud, approve payments and resolve disputes when something goes awry. For retailers, it could help determine whether an ordering mistake originated with an AI agent.

American Express confirmed to Digital Commerce 360 that Intent Intelligence has no live integrations yet. The company said publishing the framework is intended to let other payment and technology providers adopt its approach, rather than introduce new capabilities.

“Providing authorized purchase intent before an agent transacts can give issuers greater confidence that an agent is acting as a customer intended, while also helping issuers proactively manage risk and reduce the chance of costly disputes across the payments ecosystem,” Luke Gebb, head of global innovation at American Express, said in the company’s announcement.

The move comes as payment companies develop more tools for agentic commerce. With these tools, AI agents can search for products, compare prices and even complete purchases on consumers’ behalf.

Yet consumers remain cautious about giving AI control over their purchases. In a survey of 1,000 U.S. adults released in August, payments company NMI found that 58% worried that an AI shopping agent could buy the wrong item, size, color or brand. Another 60% were concerned that an agent could spend more than they intended.

Although American Express introduced Intent Intelligence in April, the latest publication makes its technical framework available for other companies to build upon. The company said the goal is to “help advance a common industry approach for intent in agentic commerce.”

What the new American Express framework means for retailers

For retailers, AI purchasing mistakes present a new challenge. A merchant could fulfill an order exactly as received, only to face a dispute because the agent bought something the shopper never requested.

That’s where a record of the shopper’s original instructions, or “purchase intent,” could help. By documenting what the customer approved, the framework offers evidence of whether the agent actually followed those instructions.

Intent Intelligence is one of five services American Express introduced in April through its Agentic Commerce Experiences (ACE) developer kit. The company said the framework “differs from current implementations” in that it shares a customer’s authorized purchase intent to the issuer “earlier in the transaction lifecycle — before an agent executes a purchase.”

American Express told Digital Commerce 360 that Intent Intelligence supports several types of purchase controls. Shoppers can set maximum spending amounts, expiration dates and merchant preferences. They can also specify when an agent should buy, such as when a product returns to stock or on Cyber Monday.

The framework also supports more complex purchases. For example, a shopper could authorize an agent to buy flight insurance only if it successfully purchases the accompanying tickets. It can also accommodate multiple transactions, such as buying shoes and socks from different retailers.

How American Express’ Intent Intelligence framework works

American Express broke down the process into four steps:

  1. “Create and confirm intent”: American Express’ Create Intent API captures what the shopper wants to buy, where the agent can shop and how much it can spend. The shopper then verifies their identity and approves the instructions the agent captured.
  2. “Establish proof of intent”: The system generates an Intent ID to identify the approved instructions, along with a Proof of Intent Token representing key purchase limits.
  3. “Scope the payment credential”: The agent can use the token to obtain a secure digital payment credential tied to the instructions. It then uses that credential at checkout instead of the shopper’s actual card number.
  4. “Apply intent throughout the transaction”: The ID and token can help check whether a purchase request matches what the shopper authorized. American Express said the records can also support “fraud prevention, authorization decisioning and dispute resolution.”

Intent Intelligence is designed to work across different agentic commerce models, regardless of who collects the shopper’s instructions, the company said. Depending on how an agent handles payments, it could send those instructions directly to a card issuer. Alternatively, a digital wallet provider or another intermediary could pass them along.

Why AI shopping errors create new payment risks

Beyond helping issuers verify purchases, the framework also ties into American Express’ plans to protect shoppers and merchants when AI agents make mistakes.

When the company introduced ACE in April, it outlined plans for what it calls “Agent Purchase Protection.” The coverage would apply to eligible transactions involving registered AI agents that use the developer kit and share authenticated purchase instructions. For merchants, the goal is to reduce chargebacks and disputes.

However, American Express confirmed to Digital Commerce 360 that the protection is not yet available. The company said it has no ACE integrations using Intent Intelligence, which is required for transactions to qualify. In the meantime, card members retain the protections and benefits available through their eligible American Express cards.

That added complexity could also affect who consumers hold responsible when something goes wrong. In NMI’s August survey, 34% of consumers said they would blame a retailer if an AI tool made a purchase before they were ready. Another 24% would hold the payment provider responsible, while 62% would blame the AI provider.

Where American Express fits in agentic commerce

American Express isn’t alone in developing tools to make AI-powered shopping more secure.

In April 2025, Visa and Mastercard each launched offerings that let developers connect AI agents to their payment networks.

Visa’s Intelligent Commerce program gives developers APIs and tools to integrate payment functions into AI agents. To support a global rollout, Visa said it was working with major technology companies, including OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Stripe and Samsung.

Meanwhile, Mastercard’s Agent Pay allows AI agents to complete purchases on users’ behalf. The program, which works with conversational AI platforms, supports both consumer and business-to-business (B2B) applications, Mastercard said.

Technology companies are developing their own standards for agentic commerce, too.

OpenAI and payments company Stripe co-developed the Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP), which lets AI agents securely connect with merchants to initiate purchases.

Meanwhile, Google’s Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) uses digitally signed records to document shoppers’ authorization. Salesforce, Shopify, Cloudflare and Etsy were among the early adopters.

Google followed in January with its Universal Commerce Protocol, developed with Shopify and other industry partners to support checkout within AI shopping experiences. More recently, electronics retailer Newegg integrated the protocol, allowing shoppers to purchase its products directly through Google’s AI Mode and Gemini experiences. Wayfair, Walmart, Macy’s and other merchants also support UCP.
